title: How a creative studio should write an about page
metaTitle: Creative studio about page: name the people
excerpt: Name who does the work and why a skeptical client should care. Skip the origin story unless it changes the decision to start a project.

faqs.question: What belongs in the opening of an about page?
faqs.answer: Who designs, who builds, and who the studio is for, in sentences a stranger can repeat. Jobs beat traits. A small team can say it is small. A collective we with no names does not prove that anyone stands behind the offer.

faqs.question: When is a founding story worth publishing?
faqs.answer: When it predicts how you will behave on the project. An archive, a store, or a small team that changed the way you decide is evidence. A city, a friendship, or a first computer is atmosphere, and it should not lead.

faqs.question: What proof should sit on the about page?
faqs.answer: One project that matches the standards you just named, captioned with the constraint and the decision. A reel does not do this. A portrait row with no link to the work feels like a casting sheet.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A creative studio about page is proof that people stand behind the offer. Name who does the work, and why a client who has already seen fifty portfolios should care. Skip the origin myth unless it changes the decision to start a project.

Biography is not the job. The buyer is checking whether judgment has a name, a practice, and a limit. A timeline from a spare room does not answer that unless the spare room is the reason they would hire you.

## People, not a myth

Open with the work the people do, in one or two sentences. Who designs. Who builds. Who the studio is for. A client should be able to repeat that without reading a paragraph about a city, a year, or a first logo.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks pages to be clear about who created them, and about the purpose of the page. An about page that hides the people behind a collective "we" and a mood photograph fails that test. So does an about page that names everyone and never says what they decide.

You can be a small studio and say so. Small is not a flaw on this page. It is information. The buyer who has hired a large firm and never met the makers is often looking for the opposite. Do not inflate the room. Do not apologize for it.

If several people do the work, give each person a job, not a trait. "Leads the interface and the type system." "Builds the production front end and the content model." Traits ("passionate," "curious," "obsessed") are interchangeable across fifty sites. Jobs are not.

## Why this buyer should care

The second part of the page is the bridge from the people to the client's risk. They are not buying a personality. They are buying a way of deciding that will show up in their site or product.

State the standards you actually use. A homepage that names one decision. A scope made of pages and states so a date can survive. Files the client owns. Words a stranger can understand. Those standards are more persuasive than a list of industries you have "touched."

Hanabi's public line is a useful model of a standard you can check: clarity over complexity, with quality, clean code, a process that can change, speed, and plain communication. Whatever your version is, put it where a client can test the work against it. If the work on the site does not obey the sentence, the sentence does not belong on the about page.

Say who you are not for, in one line. Teams that want a deck and a different vendor to build it. Projects that need a marketplace. Brands that want a new campaign every week. A refusal is more memorable than a claim of range, and it saves the call for people who fit.

Connect the page to the offer without turning it into the services page. One sentence and a link are enough. The about page convinces them the people are real. The services page tells them what to hire. Do not paste both articles into one scroll.

## When an origin earns its place

An origin earns its place when it changes the hire. You build stores because you ran one, and you still care about the week of checkout. You design editorial sites because you worked with an archive and watched readers get lost. You keep teams small because you were the unnamed person on a large account. That kind of sentence is evidence.

An origin does not earn its place when it is only atmosphere. A friendship. A favorite city. A first computer. Those details can be human in a talk. On the page, they delay the proof. The client who has seen fifty portfolios has also seen fifty founding stories. They will skip yours unless it predicts how you will behave on their project.

If you keep a short origin, put it after the standards, not before. Lead with the decision-making they came to audit. Let the story support it. A story that needs three paragraphs before the point is a speech, and this page is not a speech.

Dates and headcount are optional. If you publish them, they must be true and current. A stale "team of twelve" is worse than silence. You do not need a year of founding to look established. You need work that shows judgment, captioned, within reach of this page.

## Proof of judgment on the same page

The about page should show one piece of work, not a gallery. Choose the project that best matches the standards you just named. Caption it with the constraint and the decision. Thomas Bewick, for a studio that cares about reading. Down the Cove, for a studio that cares about a store surviving a move. Wabisabi, for a studio whose standard is restraint. The client's eye should move from the sentence to the picture and find the same idea.

Do not paste a reel here. The about page is already a claim about people. An unexplained film asks the buyer to supply the judgment themselves. They will not. They will leave with the impression of taste and no name attached to a choice.

A line about how decisions are recorded helps. Critique in the file. Comments in one place. A portal after delivery where brand files, docs, and updates stay findable. On a Hanabi project the portal is that place, so the about page is not the last time the client sees the thinking. Mention the habit, not a software tour.

If you publish names, publish the work those names touched. A portrait row with no connection to projects feels like a casting sheet. A single project with the people who made it feels like a studio.

## What to collect before you write

Do not open a blank page and reach for a tone. Collect a short pile of facts, then write only from the pile. The pile is small on purpose.

- The names you are willing to publish, and the job each person actually does on a project.
- The standards you can point to in the work, in words a client could disagree with.
- One project that proves those standards, with permission to show it.
- The clients you will not take.
- The sentence that starts a project, the same one the rest of the site uses.

If a fact is missing, leave the gap. Do not fill it with a mood. A missing portrait is better than a stock photograph of a stranger in a studio you do not have. A missing origin is better than a paragraph you would be embarrassed to read on a call.

Decide what the page will not settle. It will not explain pricing. It will not list every service. It will not carry the full case study. Those are other pages, and the about page should link to them at the moment the buyer asks. A page that tries to settle every fear becomes the long myth you were trying to avoid.

Show the draft to someone who has not worked with you. Ask them to say who does the work, who it is for, and how they would start. If they cannot, the draft is still atmosphere. Add the missing fact. Do not add another adjective. The client who has already seen fifty portfolios is a fair stand-in for that reader. They are not unkind. They are in a hurry, and they have been bored before.

## The voice of the page

Write the about page in the same sentences as the homepage. If the work is quiet, the about page cannot suddenly shout. If you use concrete nouns on the services page, do not switch to "passionate storytellers" here. The client is checking whether one studio wrote the site.

Short sentences. Names. Jobs. A limit. Read the page aloud and cut every line that could sit on a competitor's site unchanged. Those lines are the myth, even when they are flattering.

The title can be plain. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) favors a descriptive, concise title that belongs to this page alone. "About" is a weak title if every studio uses it and nothing else. A title that says who you are for is more useful, and the on-page heading can stay human.

Avoid a quote from a client you cannot stand behind, and avoid inventing one. If you have permission and a specific result, use it near the project, not as a banner. If you do not, the decision in the work is the quote.

## From the people to a project

End with the action the rest of the site uses. Start a project. One sentence on what to bring: the current site, the job that is stuck, the decision you need. The about page is often the last place a cautious buyer looks before they commit. Do not make them hunt for the button in the footer.

If you want the page built to that standard, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The useful brief is the list of people, the standards you can check, and the one project that proves them. A studio can design and build that page without turning it into a biography.

After the people are named, the buyer asks for the project in full. A portrait and one caption are not the whole proof. [Proof pages for a creative studio](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-creative-studio) are the next piece to write: the constraint, the decision, and the moment that decision shows up in the work. The about page points at them. It should not try to replace them.
